phonemes.desc: Voiced alveolar nasal [n] plus short close [ɪ], the light unstressed opening; Welsh i is close and short, never the English diphthong of 'nine'.
Voiceless alveolar sibilant [s] and short [ɪ] again — the stressed penult, where Welsh accent always falls; a clean hiss, never voiced to z.
Short open [ɛ] and final alveolar nasal [n]; the last syllable falls away unstressed, as in Welsh pen 'head'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'NISS-yen' — stress the middle syllable, keep every vowel short, and never let the s soften into a z.

kin.label: Middle Welsh
kin.form: Nissyen, the manuscript spelling of the White and Red Books, where y writes the same short vowel.

kin.label: Modern Welsh
kin.form: Nisien, the standardized modern spelling — the form the restoration takes.

kin.label: The twin pair
kin.form: Efnysien (Middle Welsh Efnissyen), his brother and antithesis; the tradition never names one without implying the other.

kin.label: Patronymic
kin.form: Nisien fab Euroswydd — son of Euroswydd, by Penarddun, and so half-brother to Brân, Branwen, and Manawydan.

pronunciation.note: Nisien is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Middle Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The manuscripts write Nissyen; the modern standard writes Nisien; only the capital distinguishes the temple form from the input. The traditional gloss 'peaceful one' suits the character exactly, but the philology behind the name is honestly uncertain, and the handbooks record rather than resolve it.

domains.title: Peace, Brother of Efnysien
domains.subtitle: The Gentle Twin of the Second Branch
domains.lead: Nisien is one half of the strangest doublet in the Mabinogi: twin brothers, sons of Euroswydd, whom the Second Branch introduces with a single matched sentence — Nisien, the good man who would make peace between two armies when they were most furious; Efnysien, who would set two loving brothers fighting to the death. The tale then gives the whole war to the cruel twin and keeps the gentle one as its standing might-have-been: peace personified, present at the court that marches to Ireland, and never once allowed to prevail.

cards.name: The Peace Between Hosts
cards.desc: The tale's whole dossier in one clause: he would bring two armies to peace at the very height of their rage.

cards.name: The Twin
cards.desc: Son of Euroswydd and Penarddun, twin of Efnysien — the gentle half of a pair the tradition built as peace and strife in one cradle.

cards.name: Euroswydd's Line
cards.desc: Half-brother to Brân the Blessed, Branwen, and Manawydan — kin to the children of Llŷr by his mother's side.

cards.name: The Road Not Taken
cards.desc: Wherever the Second Branch's counsel is weighed, Nisien is the standing alternative: the peace that was in the house and was not chosen.

symbols.name: The paired sentence
symbols.meaning: The Second Branch's balanced character note — peace and strife defined as twin brothers, one clause each

symbols.name: The twin's shadow
symbols.meaning: Efnysien's cruelty measured against Nisien's gentleness — each brother the other's definition

symbols.name: The house of Euroswydd
symbols.meaning: The second father-line of Penarddun's children — the gentler inheritance beside the children of Llŷr

symbols.name: The mutilated horses
symbols.meaning: His brother's unprovoked outrage against Matholwch's team — the act of strife that no peace in the tale can undo

symbols.name: The silent presence
symbols.meaning: The peace-maker carried with the host to Ireland and given no scene — the might-have-been that haunts the branch

mythology.lead: Nisien has the smallest dossier in the Mabinogi and the clearest definition: he exists as one half of an antithesis. The Second Branch of the Mabinogi, Branwen ferch Llŷr, names him exactly once as a character and then spends its whole length on the war his brother kindles. What survives of him is a sentence, a lineage, and a presence — and the Welsh tradition built an entire moral pole out of that spareness.

myths.title: The Two Sons of Euroswydd
myths.text:
The Second Branch introduces the twins in a single balanced construction, the most quoted sentence either brother ever gets. Nisien, the tale says, was a good man: he would bring about peace between two armies when they were at the height of their fury. Efnysien would bring about a quarrel between two brothers when they loved each other most. They are twins, sons of Euroswydd by Penarddun — and so half-brothers to Brân the Blessed, Branwen, and Manawydan, Penarddun's children by Llŷr.

The construction is the whole point: Welsh prose has no other pair like it. The tradition does not describe two temperaments; it defines two forces — peace and strife — as brothers born in one hour, and then sets them loose in the same household. Every reader of the branch knows, before the horses are harmed, exactly which twin will act and which will stand by.

myths.title: The Horses at Aberffraw
myths.text:
When Brân consents to give Branwen in marriage to Matholwch, king of Ireland, and the wedding is held at Aberffraw, it is Efnysien — insulted that the match was made without his leave — who takes revenge on the groom's horses: he cuts off their lips to the teeth, their ears to their heads, their tails to their backs, and the eyelids to the bone. The outrage becomes the war's first cause, patched over with reparation and the gift of the Cauldron of Rebirth, and reopened in Ireland when Branwen is made a scullion and struck daily in the kitchen.

Nisien's place in all this is the tale's deliberate emptiness: the peace-maker is there, kin to all parties, gifted by his own description with the one power the crisis needs — and the text never once shows him using it. The mutilation stands unappeased from its author; no embassy of Nisien's is ever recorded. The Second Branch's tragedy is written so that the reader supplies the missing twin.

myths.title: The War Over the Sea
myths.text:
Brân wades the sea at the head of the hosts of Britain, for no ship can carry him, and the war that follows destroys both kingdoms. The Irish revive their slain in the Cauldron of Rebirth, so that they rise to fight again, and the balance breaks only when Efnysien — feigning death among the corpses, flung living into the cauldron — stretches himself out and bursts it, dying in the act: the strife-twin consuming himself to undo the one weapon his own first outrage helped set in motion. Of the men of Britain only seven come home; Branwen dies of a broken heart on the shore of the Alaw.

Nisien's name is not among the dead, the seven, or the counsellors: the tale simply stops mentioning him. Scholars have long read the silence as the branch's own verdict — Mac Cana and MacKillop alike treat the twins as a personified antithesis, peace and discord hypostatized as brothers, and on that reading Nisien's function is complete the moment the paired sentence is spoken. He is not a character the tale forgot; he is the peace the tale declined.

myths.title: The Antithesis Made Flesh
myths.text:
The modern handbooks are unusually agreed about what the twins are. Mac Cana reads the pair as the Mabinogi's clearest case of abstract forces embodied as kin: the redactor names Nisien and Efnysien in one breath because they are one idea in two bodies. MacKillop's dictionary keeps both entries short for the same reason — there is no cycle, no second tale, no folklore of Nisien to collect; the dossier is the Second Branch and nothing else. Koch's encyclopedia files both under Branwen ferch Llŷr.

The names themselves resist resolution. The traditional glosses — 'peaceful one' for Nisien, 'double enemy' for Efnysien — are older scholarly convention rather than settled etymology, and the Geiriadur Prifysgol Cymru and the handbooks record the derivations as uncertain. What is certain is the structure: two names, two clauses, one cradle. The Welsh tradition made its peace-maker the way myth usually makes its gods — by naming the opposite and letting the pair do the work.

lore.syncretism: Nisien has no counterpart anywhere, and the honesty of that fact is part of his record. No Irish figure bears his name or his office: the Irish cycles know war-goddesses and peace-breaking satirists in abundance, but no personified peace-twin, and Sims-Williams's survey of Irish influence on Welsh literature — which finds deep Irish strata in the Second Branch itself, from the giant king who wades the sea to the cauldron of revival — supplies no Irish original for the sons of Euroswydd. The twins look like the Welsh redactor's own construction. The nearest comparisons are structural, drawn from inside the lexicon: his brother [[efnysien|Efnysien]], the necessary other half of the antithesis; [[manawydan|Manawydan]], his half-brother, whose own branch turns on patience and forbearance rather than force; and [[matholwch|Matholwch]], the wronged king whose horses his brother maimed. Beyond the Mabinogi the antithesis device has famous analogues — the paired forces of other traditions — but the Welsh pair needs no borrowing to explain: peace and strife as twin brothers is the sort of idea a mature prose tradition can invent in a single sentence, and the Second Branch is exactly that tradition.
lore.culturalLegacy: Nisien's afterlife is as quiet as his dossier. Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried the twins into English, and every retelling of Branwen since has kept the paired sentence — it is the one line of the Second Branch that anthologies quote whole. The scholarly tradition made the antithesis canonical: Mac Cana's study of the Mabinogi and MacKillop's dictionary fixed the reading of the twins as personified peace and strife, and the pair now serves Celtic studies as the standard example of the Welsh redactor's art of definition-by-contrast. Nisien himself never became a cult figure, a comic-book antihero, or a given name in the way louder Mabinogi figures did — Efnysien, the interesting twin, took all of that. The gentle brother's legacy is the sentence itself: in a tale about a war no one could stop, Welsh literature wrote its peace-maker in one clause and let the silence around him say the rest.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Nisien is the proof that a figure can be made of almost nothing and still be one of the most exact things in his tradition. One sentence, one lineage, no deeds — and from that the Second Branch draws a whole theology of peace: that it exists, that it lives in the same house as strife, that it can be kin to the war-makers and married into every court, and that a host can carry it over the sea and never once take it out. The tragedy of Branwen is often told as Efnysien's story, but it is just as much Nisien's: the war happens in the presence of the one man whose nature is to end it, and the text makes sure we notice by telling us his nature first and his absence always.

There is a further quietness the restoration makes visible. The name is plain ASCII — no accent to rescue, no letter to put back — because Middle Welsh wrote Nissyen and modern Welsh writes Nisien, and the keyboard never lost anything. Tier 2 says only that. The tradition said the rest nine centuries ago: the gentle twin, defined once, standing at the shoulder of the war for its whole length, the road the house of Llŷr did not take. Every court has a Nisien. The Mabinogi's question is why he is so seldom asked.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Middle Welsh form is Nisien (manuscript Nissyen) — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Middle Welsh was written in the Latin alphabet in the medieval Welsh bookhand; the earlier epigraphic scripts of Britain, the Latin and ogham memorial stones, name no figure of the Mabinogi. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: nisien.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Nisien is a purely textual figure: no inscription, votive deposit, or cult site names him, and the early inscribed stones of Wales — the Latin and ogham memorials of roughly the fifth to seventh centuries — record personal names in funerary formulae, not theonyms or tale-figures. His evidence is manuscript evidence. The Four Branches survive complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6; the tales' date of composition is argued rather than documented, with current scholarship generally holding a range around 1060–1120. The geography of his branch is real: Aberffraw, where the wedding and the outrage are set, was the historic principal seat of the kings and later princes of Gwynedd on Anglesey, and the Alaw, where Branwen dies of her broken heart, is an Anglesey river. The giant who wades the sea and the cauldron of revival belong to the tale's mythic furniture; the courts and the crossings are drawn from the Welsh world the redactor knew.
